claims.text: Components used in hot-dip aluminum plating are currently made from conventional engineering metals such as standard steels or nickel-based superalloys.
Conventional engineering metals used in this equipment are rapidly corroded by high-temperature liquid aluminum.
Chromium and hafnium are refractory elements that can be incorporated into refractory high-entropy alloys.
Refractory high-entropy alloys have properties that make them potential structural materials for elevated-temperature service.
A Cr- and Hf-containing refractory high-entropy alloy can be prepared by powder metallurgy or spark plasma sintering.
Hot-dip aluminum plating exposes equipment parts to molten aluminum at approximately 660°C for prolonged periods.
Adding chromium and hafnium to the proposed alloy will promote preferential oxidation during molten-aluminum exposure.
The proposed alloy will form Cr2O3 and HfO2 on its surface at approximately 660°C.
The resulting oxide scale will be dense and adherent.
The resulting oxide scale will be self-healing.
The compact oxide layer will act as a diffusion barrier between molten aluminum and the underlying alloy.
The oxide diffusion barrier will prevent or reduce corrosion of the underlying material by molten aluminum.
The proposed alloy will have a significantly lower molten-aluminum corrosion rate than conventional materials.
Using the proposed alloy will extend the service life of dipping and plating equipment parts.
The long-term stability of the protective oxide under thermal cycling and contaminants is uncertain.
The magnitude of the expected corrosion-rate reduction and service-life extension has not been quantified.
